claims_summary.note: The 47 were found by a keyword filter (ledger/measured/empirical...). 36 are real market claims, 1 is true by arithmetic (its audit is still a test), 1 is about human analysts, 9 describe the book's own bookkeeping.

F1.name: Gap behaviour
F1.plain: Do the four kinds of price gaps really behave differently, and do 'common' gaps fill fast?
F1.test: Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier time-to-fill per gap class with a log-rank test; fill-within-k-bars share with Wilson intervals using effective sample size; Kruskal-Wallis on forward outcome (ATR units, 5/10/20 bars) across the four classes.
F1.gates: G1 event study per class, then G2-G4; every rate split by regime state (X-9).
F1.table: gap class x break outcome (E-10..E-14), E-9 fill clocks

F2.name: Method and doctrine bake-offs
F2.plain: Where the book offers several ways to do one thing (confirm a break, measure a pullback, rank references, set a target, reverse after a trend dies), which way actually works best?
F2.test: Run every option on the same events; score each by outcome after costs (triple-barrier result in ATR, confirmation lag, false-confirm rate). Compare options with Hansen SPA / White Reality Check across the whole option family; the winner must also pass deflated Sharpe with every option counted as a trial; out-of-sample check by purged combinatorial cross-validation.
F2.gates: G1 per option -> G2 CPCV -> G5 deflated Sharpe (trial count = all options) -> G6 family SPA.
F2.table: per-option honesty columns (cfm.mode, retr.method, ref.rankOrder, brk.objOdds)

F3.name: Base rates vs the classical books
F3.plain: Classic authors (mainly Bulkowski) quote numbers such as 'price comes back to test the break about 60% of the time'. Are those numbers true on our data?
F3.test: Share of events with the outcome, with a Wilson interval widened for overlap (effective sample size or block bootstrap); one-sided binomial test against the quoted seed number or 50%; a 'seed vs loop' column that shows both.
F3.gates: G1 (base rate with honest interval); split by reference type x grade x regime state.
F3.table: brk.entryOdds, A-1 retest base rates, P-9 SEED-EXT vs loop column

F4.name: Does a label add information?
F4.plain: The book attaches labels to events (pressure building, volume drying up, attempt number, pattern name, whipsaw, moving-average bounce). Does an event with the label turn out differently from the same kind of event without it?
F4.test: Conditional lift: outcome with label minus outcome without, same reference type and regime; block-bootstrap interval; bar-permutation p-value; for pattern names, a nested model test (plain break chain vs chain + name) judged on out-of-sample log-loss.
F4.gates: G1 lift -> G2/G3 stability -> G4 permutation; regime column mandatory.
F4.table: vol.dryLift, vol.breakLift, level.testOdds, brk.gapEntryOdds, pattern rows

F5.name: Regime conditioning
F5.plain: The book's central empirical claim: the break rules earn money in trending markets, lose in choppy ones, and net to zero when mixed. Is that true on real prices?
F5.test: Stratified event study per regime state (TRENDING / RANGING / TREND-IN-RANGE / TRANSITIONAL); interaction test and Cochran's Q for 'the effect differs by state'; pooled interval must include zero while at least one state's interval excludes it; dead-zone check = outcome as a function of bars since the last regime change.
F5.gates: Full ladder G0-G6 per state; this is the loop's planned Sprint 3 'Condition on Regime'.
F5.table: regime columns on every table (X-9), regime.disputeOdds, inversion columns

F6.name: Higher timeframe
F6.plain: Does trading in the direction of the weekly chart really help, and does a daily event give useful early warning of a weekly one?
F6.test: Outcome difference HTF-ALIGNED minus HTF-OPPOSED (block bootstrap); WARN lead time via Kaplan-Meier with precision/recall of warnings; an equivalence test (TOST) decides when the alignment column 'reads flat' and the doctrine must demote.
F6.gates: G1-G4 per reference type x grade x state.

F7.name: Independent witnesses
F7.plain: Are two indicators really two opinions, or one opinion counted twice? And when ADX and the price-based trend call disagree, which one is usually early?
F7.test: Spearman rank correlation with effective-sample-size interval; event agreement rate; conditional lift of B given A; lead-lag = sign test on which series changes state first in disagreement episodes; a Monte Carlo demonstration that stacking correlated signals inflates confidence.
F7.gates: Audit, not a promotion ladder: result stamps each pair ONE-WITNESS or independent (I-2 audit.pairs).

F8.name: Other markets
F8.plain: Do rules calibrated on large US stocks work on ETFs (then FX, crypto)? Does 'oversold' mean the same on an index as on a single stock?
F8.test: Frequency comparison (share of days RSI14 < 30 on the index vs its members, two-proportion test with effective sample size); percentile-threshold calibration (do percentile lines fire at their nominal rate out-of-sample, binomial coverage test); out-of-class degradation ratio (walk-forward efficiency style) with interval.
F8.gates: Per-class ladder (U-9): a pass on stocks transfers to nothing; ETF first (R8 U-R1).

F9.name: Risk profiles and sizing
F9.plain: Do the three appetites (conservative, moderate, aggressive) really differ in results, and does betting more on better-graded setups help?
F9.test: Profile backtests on identical events (invariance check: 100% same events); expectancy, drawdown, deflated Sharpe per profile; grade monotonicity with Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test (A > B > C); graded sizing vs flat sizing compared on deflated-Sharpe-adjusted difference.
F9.gates: G2/G3 on each profile's return series; G5 with profiles counted as trials.

F10.name: Trap setups
F10.plain: The book is most confident about traps (fakeouts, springs, gap traps). Those deserve the strictest test.
F10.test: Full ladder per setup class with the lockbox (never-touched final years) spent only at promotion; pre-registered before any run because priors are strongest here.
F10.table: A-10 aftermath ledger (fake.setupOdds, spring/upthrust odds, gap-trap odds)

F11.name: Not a market claim (design or bookkeeping)
F11.plain: These sentences were caught by the keyword filter but make no claim about markets. They describe how the book keeps its books. They need a mechanical check, not statistics.
F11.test: Compile / audit checks: two independent implementations agree bar-for-bar; ledger audit (no duplicate records of one price, no orphan floors, no cross-frame padding); publication lint (every printed rate points to a ledger cell with a date and a regime column; no size multiplier on an unmeasured stamp).
F11.gates: G0 compile gate and code lint; no statistical gate.

F12.name: A claim about people
F12.plain: 'Hand-drawn trendlines always end up agreeing with the person drawing them.' This is about analysts, not prices.
F12.test: Inter-rater study: several independent drawers (or randomized hand-fit algorithms) on the same charts; dispersion of slope/intercept and Fleiss' kappa on break calls, versus swing-anchored lines (which should agree 100%). Low priority: the rule does not depend on it.
